\[f_1(X,Y)=X^2+5Y^2,\qquad f_2(X,Y)=2X^2+2XY+3Y^2.\]
Moreover, the proper classes of these forms form a group under Gauss composition; here f_1 is the identity and f_2\circ f_2=f_1. (This follows directly from the usual composition law, since the reduced forms of discriminant -20 are precisely the two displayed forms.)

Thus, if n_i is represented by a form Q_i of discriminant -20, choose a proper equivalence Q_i\sim f_{j_i}. Proper equivalence preserves represented integers, so n_i is represented by f_{j_i}. Gauss composition gives a form Q_3 of discriminant -20 whose class is f_{j_1}\circ f_{j_2}, and the composition identity gives that the product of represented values is represented by Q_3. Hence n_1n_2 is represented by an integral quadratic form of discriminant -20. Therefore n_1n_2 is good. \(\square\)

Indeed, for a reduced form one has |b|\le a\le c; the equation 4ac-b^2=20 then leaves only these two possibilities, up to proper equivalence.

Both displayed forms are primitive, and their proper classes constitute the class group of discriminant -20. The composition theorem says: if Q_1 represents n_1 and Q_2 represents n_2, then Q_1\circ Q_2 represents n_1n_2. Applying this to forms representing the given good numbers produces an integral form Q_3 with discriminant -20 representing n_1n_2. Consequently n_1n_2 is good by definition. \(\square\)

Let \(n_1=Q_1(x_1,y_1)\) and \(n_2=Q_2(x_2,y_2)\), with \(Q_i\) integral and \(\operatorname{disc}(Q_i)=-20\). Since \(-20\) is a fundamental discriminant, every integral form of discriminant \(-20\) is primitive: if a common divisor \(d>1\) divided its coefficients, then \(d^2\mid20\); hence \(d=2\), which would make the reduced discriminant divided by 4 equal to \(-5\), impossible modulo 4.

Therefore Gauss's composition theorem applies to \(Q_1,Q_2\). It supplies an integral primitive form \(Q_3\) of the same discriminant and integers \(X,Y\) (obtained from the composition construction applied to \((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\)) such that
\[Q_3(X,Y)=Q_1(x_1,y_1)Q_2(x_2,y_2)=n_1n_2.\]
Thus \(Q_3\) has integer coefficients, discriminant \(-20\), and represents the positive integer \(n_1n_2\). Hence that product is good. \(\square\)

We use the standard composition theorem for primitive integral binary quadratic forms: if primitive forms of the same discriminant \(D\) represent integers \(r\) and \(s\), then their Gauss composition is a primitive integral form of discriminant \(D\) representing \(rs\).

First, every integral form \([a,b,c]\) of discriminant \(-20\) is primitive. If \(d=\gcd(a,b,c)>1\), then \(d^2\mid20\), so \(d=2\). Dividing the coefficients by 2 would give an integral form of discriminant \(-5\), but an integral discriminant has the form \(b'^2-4a'c'\), which is congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 4, whereas \(-5\equiv3\pmod4\), a contradiction.

Now let \(n_1,n_2\) be good, represented respectively by forms \(Q_1,Q_2\) of discriminant \(-20\). The preceding paragraph makes both forms primitive, so composition yields a primitive integral form \(Q_3\) with discriminant \(-20\) and integers \(X,Y\) satisfying
\[Q_3(X,Y)=Q_1(\cdot)Q_2(\cdot)=n_1n_2.\]
Therefore the product is represented in the required form and is good. \(\square\)
